newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel to discuss reserves with Tietmeyer on Thursday. [CORRECTED 21:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Waigel to discuss reserves with Tietmeyer on Thursday. [CORRECTED 21:00 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects headline and throughout to make clear Waigel referred to reserves in general and not specifically the Bundesbank's gold reserves).
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Wednesday he would meet on Thursday with Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer to discuss Bonn's plans to revalue the German central bank's reserves.

Waigel told reporters after a meeting of Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) deputies that he believed Bonn and the Bundesbank, which had been at bitter odds over the plan, "were on the way to solving the issue".
"I can say that I will meet with Mr. Tietmeyer tomorrow and we are on the way to solving the issue over the revaluation of the Bundesbank's reserves," Waigel said.

Waigel also said Germany can meet entry criteria for the single European currency laid out in the Maastricht Treaty with a debt of slightly above 60 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which is the level outlined in the treaty.
"We in Germany can meet (the criteria) with a slight overshooting of the debt criterion," Waigel told reporters.
Tietmeyer said earlier on Wednesday in Cologne that he would meet with Waigel sometime this week and expected a final clarification on the revaluation issue.
There is no Bundesbank council meeting this week. Council meetings generally take place every second Thursday.

Bonn and the Bundesbank had a public fight over Waigel's plans to revalue gold and currency assets, which are priced well below market value, and use the booked profits to cut Bonn's debt and help Germany qualify for the single European currency.
The Bundesbank lashed out at Bonn, saying its independence had been attacked and Germany's credibility as a hardliner on EMU undermined.
Waigel retreated from his plan to obtain the funds in 1997, the year when the financial health of European nations seeking to join the euro in 1999 will be reviewed.
Independent economists expect the Bundesbank to go along to a degree with a revised revaluation plan and transfer a portion of the proceeds to Bonn but not in 1997.
